source: Sungrow LC200/LC300 fault & alarm guide, 8-1-1-0
cause: Raised while at least one PCS is still communicating and every PCS is either faulted or out of contact with the LC. Checked every 300 ms; clears by itself as soon as any PCS recovers.
remedy: This names the device, not the problem. Open Running information - Energy storage converter information on the LC and read the whole-machine fault status to find which PCS is faulted and why; work that fault. If only some PCS units are affected the LC raises "PCS unit fault" as an alarm instead of this fault.

source: Sungrow LC200/LC300 fault & alarm guide, 8-1-1-2
cause: Raised while at least one BSC is still communicating and every BSC is either faulted or out of contact with the LC. Checked every 300 ms; clears as soon as any BSC recovers.
remedy: Open Battery system controller information on the LC, find the specific BSC fault and work that. This alarm only says which controller saw it.

source: Sungrow LC200/LC300 fault & alarm guide, 8-1-1-6
cause: A node configured as a fault type is open or closed against its expected state. Checked every 300 ms.
action: Fault reported, system stops, and whatever the node is configured to trigger runs.
remedy: Open Node information on the LC to find which node. Then confirm at the hardware why the DIN input reads wrong. Usual causes: the node device itself has failed; a poor contact in the wiring is giving a false report; the controller hardware is damaged. For a linked DI/DO node (fan supply circuit, for instance) the fault depends on input and output agreeing, not on the default state.

source: Sungrow LC200/LC300 fault & alarm guide, 8-1-1-7
cause: No unit can run although nothing is faulted — a healthy PCS whose BSC is faulted, or a healthy BSC whose PCS is faulted.
remedy: Clear the "PCS unit fault" and "BSC unit fault" alarms first. Then check whether a BSC is blocked from starting on low temperature: when the coldest cell in every battery unit is below the minimum start temperature the BSC reads start-inhibited. On 2.0HX check that the PCS-CMU signal receive point is not disabled — a disabled point alone makes the LC report this.

source: Sungrow LC200/LC300 fault & alarm guide, 8-1-1-8
cause: The LC, or any BSC, has its "system emergency stop" node in fault.
action: Fault reported, system stops, plus whatever the emergency-stop node is configured to trigger.
remedy: Treat as a node fault: confirm at the hardware why the DIN input reads wrong. Usual causes are the node device itself, a poor contact giving a false report, or damaged controller hardware.

source: Sungrow LC200/LC300 fault & alarm guide, 8-1-1-1 / 8-1-2-3; Site practice — Tashkent
cause: Every PCS has lost contact with the LC (fault), or only some have (alarm). With GOOSE enabled both GOOSE and Modbus are judged.
action: Fault reported, system stops. The alarm variant only reports.
remedy: On site this is usually the cable: reseat it first, and a restart often clears it. If it persists, replace the RJ-45, and as a last resort the communication board on the PCS. A useful check: if only one LC on the block shows the fault while the other LC on the same block is healthy, the problem is on that leg, not upstream. Vendor steps: confirm the PCS IP configuration in the LC; log into the LC with xshell and ping the PCS; with GOOSE enabled verify the PCS GOOSE frames arrive and their MAC matches the LC. Note that after a program restart with GOOSE enabled this fault clears itself in about 3 minutes while the protocol loads — that is normal. Recorded cases: a CMU upgrade restarting the CMU briefly drops PCS power and the socket disconnects; and duplicate MAC addresses on two PCS units, which kept them from being online at the same time.

source: Sungrow LC200/LC300 fault & alarm guide, 8-1-1-3 / 8-1-2-6; Site practice — Tashkent
cause: Every BSC has lost contact with the LC (fault), or only some have (alarm).
action: Fault reported, system stops. The alarm variant only reports.
remedy: Check the communication cable first — reseat, then restart. Confirm the BSC IP configuration in the LC and that IP, port and Modbus address match the equipment as wired; the BSC-to-PCS mapping must be right too. Log into the LC with xshell and ping the BSC. Recorded case: the BSC simply lost power — its DC24V came from a supply board whose DC input breaker had been left off, so it kept rebooting.

source: Site practice — Tashkent; Sungrow LC200/LC300 fault & alarm guide (ethernet troubleshooting)
cause: The BSC cannot talk to the PCS.
remedy: Same repair as the other communication faults: reseat the cable, restart, then replace the RJ-45 and finally the PCS communication board. Check IP, port and Modbus address against the equipment as wired. If only one LC on the block is affected and the other is healthy, the fault is on that leg.

source: Site practice — Tashkent; Sungrow LC200/LC300 fault & alarm guide, 8-1-2-6
cause: The BSC cannot talk to the LC.
remedy: Reseat the cable and restart; then RJ-45, then the communication board. Confirm IP, port and Modbus address, and that the BSC-PCS mapping is configured.

source: Sungrow LC200/LC300 fault & alarm guide, 8-1-2-8 … 8-1-2-11
cause: The LC system alarm word, which carries several alarms at once. Among them are the SOC limit alarms: SOC upper limit level 1 and 2, SOC lower limit level 1 and 2. Each fires when a rack's online SOC passes the threshold for longer than the configured SOC control delay.
action: Alarm reported only — the system keeps running.
remedy: Usually nothing. The SOC limit alarms clear on their own: discharging below the upper-limit recovery value, or charging above the lower-limit recovery value, ends them. They therefore appear on every normal charge to the limit, which is why this word dominates the alarm hours. Read the specific alarm behind it before treating it as a fault.

source: Sungrow LC200/LC300 fault & alarm guide, 8-1-2-7
cause: A node configured as an alarm type is open or closed against its expected state.
action: Alarm reported, plus whatever the node is configured to trigger.
remedy: Check against the node fault/alarm list, then treat as a node fault: the node device itself, a poor contact giving a false report, or damaged controller hardware.

source: Sungrow LC200/LC300 fault & alarm guide, 8-1-1-12 / 8-1-2-27
cause: Any of: a fire dry-node whose configuration and actual state disagree; the composite detector reporting abnormal; the combustible-gas detector reporting a level 1 or 2 concentration alarm.
remedy: Find which of the three actually triggered and work that one. The detector-and-gas-release alarm is a collection: fire probe tube signal, aerosol trigger, fire system alarm, fire system fault, gas release, smoke and temperature detectors, composite detector alarm or its comms alarm, gas concentration alarm, gas detector alarm or its comms alarm.

source: Sungrow LC200/LC300 fault & alarm guide, 8-1-2-16 / 8-1-1-12
cause: The combustible-gas detector reports a level 1 or level 2 concentration alarm.
action: Rolled into the firefighting system fault — system stops.
remedy: Treat as a real gas event until proven otherwise. Then follow the general sub-device alarm handling: verify the detector itself and its communication before assuming the reading is false.

source: Site practice — Tashkent (measured over six months)
cause: A general input signal on the BSC. It is raised beside the fault that actually occurred rather than naming one: of 5,668 occurrences only 2% had no other alarm on the same block at the same time.
action: Reported as a fault; the hours it accumulates largely duplicate those of the fault it accompanies.
remedy: Do not work this alarm on its own. Look at what else was alarming on the block at the same moment — most often a BSC-PCS communication fault, and in about one case in ten the firefighting system. Where it truly stands alone it is the only evidence there is, and then it is worth investigating.

If the fault repeatedly occurs (If the busbar voltage exceeds 1650V, the input side switch will be locked. To check and reset the switch, switch off the machine manually.): 1.Check whether the battery voltage is higher than the maximum allowable voltage. If so, the fault occurs because of battery failure. 2.Check the protection parameter settings. 3.If the fault persists, please contact Sungrow Customer Service(+86 - 400 119 7799).

If so, the fault occurs because of insufficient battery voltage. 2.Check the protection parameter settings. 3.If the fault persists, please contact Sungrow Customer Service(+86 - 400 119 7799).

source: Sungrow BSC200/300 fault & alarm handling table (模组过温)

If the fault repeatedly occurs: 1.Check whether the ambient temperature of the PCS is excessively high. 2.Check whether the device is placed in a well-ventilated place. 3.Check whether the machine is exposed to direct sunlight. Shield the machine if it is under direct sunlight. 4.Check whether the fan is running properly. Replace the fan if necessary. 5.If the fault persists, please contact Sungrow Customer Service(+86 - 400 119 7799).

source: Sungrow BSC/DCDC guide, 5-2-2 DCDC fault-code decoding; 8-2-2-5
cause: The BSC records a DCDC fault only down to the major fault class, never the sub-fault. The DCDC alarm is raised when some but not all DCDCs in a battery unit are faulted; when every one is, it becomes a fault instead.
action: Alarm reported; clears by itself once every DCDC in the unit is healthy again.
remedy: To read the BSC record: convert the DCDC fault code to binary — each bit is one major fault class — and take the DCDC fault position as the highest index among the faulted units. Code 3 (0011) with position 4 means that among the first four DCDCs something reported a battery fault and a system fault; code 35 (0010 0011) with position 7 adds a battery alarm among the first seven. Then work the DCDC itself — the BSC entry alone does not name the sub-fault.

source: Sungrow BSC/DCDC guide, 8-2-2-9
cause: Any DCDC in the battery unit has lost communication with the BSC.
action: Alarm reported; clears when every DCDC in the unit is back.
remedy: Check the DCDC is powered. Check the communication cabling per the manual, and that the DCDC addresses configured in the BSC are right; log into the BSC with xshell and ping the DCDC. Recorded case: repeated alarms on the 1# DCDC of every cabin turned out to be its DSP losing power, so the ARM kept resetting and the DCDC kept restarting — the supply breaker for that DCDC had been switched off on site because circulating current from disabled SOC balancing was draining it into the others. Restoring the supply ended the alarms.

source: Sungrow BSC/DCDC guide, 8-1-1-22
cause: Fewer DCDCs are online than the configured minimum.
remedy: First check the setting itself — the configured minimum may be higher than the number of DCDCs actually installed. Then check DCDC-to-BSC communication for anything that has dropped a unit offline. Only if setting and network are both sound is the DCDC itself at fault.
